clue.text: Maiden with chaps in bed – ‘Here’s How’ in French

definitions.note: the answer is the French word for 'how'

indicators.note: one thing lying in another is held inside it, so the outer word wraps the rest

blocks.note: M is the cricket abbreviation for a maiden over
chaps are men
a cot is a small bed

explanation.surface: A girl with some fellows in bed, and a French phrase-book heading for the occasion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'with' just joins the maiden to the chaps; together they go inside the cot. The definition is the playful cue that COMMENT is how the French say 'how'.
explanation.definitionFit: In French, the interrogative adverb meaning 'in what way' is spelt exactly like the English word for a remark.

clue.text: Copy in bed

blocks.note: first meaning: to copy another's work dishonestly
second meaning: a baby's cot

explanation.walkthrough: 'in' reads like a place, but it only joins two separate meanings of one short word.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is both a verb for plagiarising or cheating from someone else's work and a noun for a child's barred sleeping cot.

clue.text: Description of lawyer meanly inferred, possibly, by defendant, initially

indicators.note: 'possibly' means in some other possible form, so the letters may be rearranged
'initially' means at the start, so only the opening letter is kept

blocks.note: taken as written, as anagram fodder
the first letter of defendant

explanation.surface: Someone in court sneers that the defendant has only grudgingly implied something about a lawyer.
explanation.walkthrough: In British courts barristers politely refer to opposing counsel with this phrase. The fourteen letters of 'meanly inferred' plus the defendant's initial make the fifteen needed.
explanation.definitionFit: This is the conventional courtroom courtesy phrase by which a barrister refers to another lawyer in the case.

clue.text: Record expressions of impatience for ages

blocks.note: an EP is an extended-play record
'och' is a Scottish exclamation of irritation

explanation.surface: Someone keeps tutting impatiently for ages, and the noise gets recorded.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Och' is the Scots exclamation of annoyance, made plural here.
explanation.definitionFit: Epochs and ages are both long, distinct periods of history or geological time, so they are synonyms.

clue.text: Receiving thanks, man!

blocks.note: ta is informal British for thanks
a king is a chess man

explanation.surface: Someone accepts a gift and says 'thanks, man!'
explanation.walkthrough: 'man' sounds like a casual address, but it is a chess piece; ta is British slang for thanks.
explanation.definitionFit: Taking and receiving are both present participles describing getting hold of something offered, so they are synonyms.

clue.text: Vegetable to cut, cut and cut

indicators.note: to cut something is to shorten it, so a word loses its final letter

blocks.note: to pare is to cut, and here it is docked of its last letter
a snip is a cut

explanation.surface: Kitchen instructions for chopping a vegetable: cut, cut and cut again.
explanation.walkthrough: The three 'cut's do different jobs: the first is part of 'to cut' (PARE), the second trims it to PAR, the third is SNIP.
explanation.definitionFit: A parsnip is a pale root vegetable related to the carrot, so it is an example of the category.

clue.text: Source of dates from Lampeter

indicators.note: something made from raw material is formed out of it, so the letters are remade into something new

blocks.note: taken as written: a small town in Wales

explanation.surface: Dates said to come from a Welsh university town.
explanation.walkthrough: Lampeter is a Welsh town; its letters rearrange. The 'dates' look historical, but they are fruit.
explanation.definitionFit: Dates are the fruit of the date palm, so a palm tree is where that fruit grows and comes from.

clue.text: Memo – ‘What’s left when adult leaves?’

indicators.note: when someone leaves they go away, so that letter departs from the word

blocks.note: the remainder is what is left over
A is the film-certificate abbreviation for adult

explanation.surface: A note asking what happens to the remaining staff when a grown-up departs.
explanation.walkthrough: Take the A out of REMAINDER.
explanation.definitionFit: A memo is a short written note jogging someone's memory, which is what a reminder is.

clue.text: Plays for England here – and the rest of us

blocks.note: surface reading: a stadium where a sportsman represents the national team
setter's reading: dramas staged for the whole country, owned by the public, so the playhouse belongs to everyone

explanation.walkthrough: 'Plays for England' suggests a footballer or cricketer, but the plays are dramas. The National Theatre is a state-funded London playhouse on the South Bank, run on behalf of the whole nation, hence 'the rest of us'.
explanation.definitionFit: It is Britain's publicly funded flagship playhouse, staging drama on behalf of the entire country.

clue.text: Close partner, yet not so

indicators.note: 'not so' says things are not as stated, so these letters are not in their given order

blocks.note: taken as written, ignoring the comma

explanation.surface: Someone is close to a partner, and yet not really close at all.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Close partner' reads as one phrase about intimacy, but 'Close' alone is the definition, an adverb meaning almost.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is an informal adverb for almost, describing something approaching but not quite reaching a mark.

clue.text: One grand by John Snow house

blocks.note: I is the Roman numeral one
G is short for a grand, a thousand
john is slang for a lavatory, as is loo

explanation.surface: A splendid house belonging to Jon Snow, the newsreader or the Game of Thrones hero.
explanation.walkthrough: 'John Snow' looks like a name, but the split is John (a toilet) and 'Snow house' the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: An igloo is a dome-shaped Inuit shelter built from blocks of packed snow, literally a dwelling of snow.

clue.text: Juliet’s follower encountered sapper at a distance

blocks.note: in the NATO alphabet Kilo follows Juliet
met means encountered
sappers are the Royal Engineers, RE

explanation.surface: Romeo, Juliet's follower, spots an army engineer from afar.
explanation.walkthrough: Juliet suggests Romeo, but in the radio alphabet the next word is Kilo.
explanation.definitionFit: A kilometre is a metric unit measuring length, one thousand metres, so it names a specific span of space.

clue.text: March newspaper

blocks.note: first meaning: a famous military march by John Philip Sousa
second meaning: a leading American daily paper

explanation.walkthrough: 'March' looks like the month or a protest, but it is a piece of music, Sousa's 1889 march named after the paper.
explanation.definitionFit: The name belongs both to Sousa's well-known brass-band composition and to the American daily published in the capital.

clue.text: Liver and lime mixed with cold pasta

indicators.note: things mixed together are jumbled, so the letters lose their order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written
C is the abbreviation for cold, as on taps

explanation.surface: An odd recipe: liver and lime tossed through cold pasta.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cold' looks like a description of the pasta, but it supplies only its abbreviation to the mix.
explanation.definitionFit: Vermicelli is a very thin Italian noodle, so it is a specific kind of the general food category.

clue.text: Sea eagle in summer nest

indicators.note: 'in' says the letters sit inside the following words, already there

blocks.note: found across the two words

explanation.surface: A sea eagle sitting in its nest during the summer.
explanation.walkthrough: The bird is literally sitting in the nest letters: summER NEst.
explanation.definitionFit: The erne is the white-tailed eagle, a large raptor of coasts, a crossword favourite among birds.

clue.text: Composer who repairs the box, we’re told

indicators.note: what we are told we hear spoken, so the sound matters rather than the spelling

blocks.note: the box is slang for television, and a telly man fixes it

explanation.surface: A composer who moonlights fixing television sets, or so the gossip goes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The box' and 'telly' are both British slang for the television set.
explanation.definitionFit: Georg Philipp Telemann was a prolific German Baroque composer, a contemporary of Bach and Handel.

clue.text: Bunthorne’s Bride is game

blocks.note: first meaning: the subtitle of a Gilbert and Sullivan comic opera
second meaning: a card game for one player

explanation.walkthrough: The italics mark a title: the full title of the Gilbert and Sullivan operetta is 'Patience, or Bunthorne's Bride'. Patience is also the British name for solitaire.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names both the 1881 Savoy opera with that subtitle and the solo card game Americans call solitaire.

clue.text: Postpone work on aircraft delivery

blocks.note: the de Havilland Moth was a classic light aircraft
in cricket a delivery is a ball bowled

explanation.surface: A delivery of aircraft parts is delayed, holding up the work.
explanation.walkthrough: 'work on aircraft' wants to be one phrase, but 'Postpone work on' is the definition. A delivery is a cricket term for a single bowled ball.
explanation.definitionFit: To mothball a project is an idiom for shelving or suspending it, storing it away for possible later revival.

clue.text: Press and TV nonsense repelled broker

indicators.note: something repelled is driven back, so these letters run backwards

blocks.note: the press and television are the media
rot is nonsense

explanation.surface: A dealmaker who pushed back against rubbish from the newspapers and television.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Press and TV' together give one word.
explanation.definitionFit: To broker a deal is to negotiate between sides, and a broker in that sense is a go-between or intermediary.

clue.text: Walkway seen from Piraeus to Athens

indicators.note: something seen from within a stretch of text is visible in it already

blocks.note: spanning the end of the port name and the next words

explanation.surface: A covered walkway glimpsed on the road from the port of Piraeus to Athens.
explanation.walkthrough: PiraeuS TO Athens holds it; Piraeus is the port of Athens.
explanation.definitionFit: A stoa is an ancient Greek covered colonnade or portico used as a public walkway, so the scene fits.

clue.text: What’ll suggest fencing material?

indicators.note: spoken words suggest another word by their sound alone, not their spelling

blocks.note: the contraction said quickly

explanation.surface: A question: which material should we use for the fence?
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark makes it look like a query, but 'What'll' is the sound of the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Wattle is woven hurdle-work of rods and twigs, traditionally used for fences and walls, as in wattle and daub.

clue.text: In haste, pupils advance

indicators.note: 'In' says the letters sit inside the following words, already present

blocks.note: spanning the comma

explanation.surface: Hurrying schoolchildren move forward in a rush.
explanation.walkthrough: haSTE PUPils holds it, across the comma.
explanation.definitionFit: To step up is a phrasal verb for moving forward or increasing, so it matches advancing as a verb.

clue.text: Eats with chips.? No sir! Not normally oggies

indicators.note: something not done normally is done in an irregular way, so the letters come out of order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A diner is told firmly they will not get chips with their pies.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Oggy' is Cornish and Devon slang for a pasty, a pastry case filled with meat and vegetables; 'with' joins the fodder pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Oggies is the dialect name in south-west England for the traditional baked pastry turnover of Cornwall.

clue.text: Additional luxurious fabric is trimmed

indicators.note: trimming cuts off an edge, so the word loses its last letter

blocks.note: plush is a rich fabric with a long soft pile

explanation.surface: Extra rich fabric has its edges cut away.
explanation.walkthrough: Plush is a velvety cloth with a long pile; trimmed, it loses its last letter.
explanation.definitionFit: As an adjective, plus means extra or added on, as in a plus point, matching the sense of additional.

clue.text: New militia lacking its leader is deployed to ambush

indicators.note: lacking a leader means missing the front, so the first letter goes
troops deployed are spread out into fresh positions, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written
militia without its first letter

explanation.surface: A fresh, leaderless militia is sent out to set up an ambush.
explanation.walkthrough: 'New' reads as an adjective for the militia, but its letters are part of the mix.
explanation.definitionFit: To lie in wait is an idiom for hiding ready to attack by surprise, exactly what ambushing someone involves.

clue.text: Piano, not in time, backing viola’s piece

indicators.note: backing means moving backwards, so the letters run in reverse

blocks.note: p is the musical abbreviation for piano, softly
not on time is late

explanation.surface: A pianist out of time accompanying a viola player's solo.
explanation.walkthrough: The viola is not the instrument but the flower, a pansy relative; the musical surface hides that.
explanation.definitionFit: A viola is a garden flower, and one of the coloured leaf-like parts of its bloom is a piece of it.

clue.text: Forever remain popular, a touch dizzy and healthy

indicators.note: only a touch of a word is a tiny part of it, its first letter

blocks.note: in means fashionable, popular
the first letter of dizzy
well means in good health

explanation.surface: A wish to stay popular for ever, slightly giddy and in good health.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dizzy' sounds like a description, but only its first letter is used.
explanation.definitionFit: To indwell is a literary verb for abiding permanently within, as a spirit dwells inside a person.

clue.text: Train former journalists

blocks.note: ex means former
journalists collectively are the press

explanation.surface: Coaching people who used to be reporters.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Train' looks like a verb, to coach; it is the noun, a fast railway service.
explanation.definitionFit: An express is a fast passenger train that stops at only a few stations, so it is an example of the vehicle.
